newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-CARLING CHOOSES PERFECT MOMENT TO RETIRE.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-CARLING CHOOSES PERFECT MOMENT TO RETIRE.

text.p: With a sense of timing which rarely deserted him either on or off the field, former England captain Will Carling has chosen the perfect moment to retire from international rugby.
Unavailable for the forthcoming British Lions tour of South Africa, Carling had planned to decide over the northern summer whether he would continue at international level.
Instead he has decided to quit at the top, while still able to command an automatic England place.
"I believe it is far better to let go than have it ripped from you," Carling wrote in his weekly newspaper column. "You know inside when it is time to go.
"You just lose that edge, the drive that forced you ahead of others."
Carling took over unexpectedly as national captain in 1988, a year after England had stumbled ignominiously out of the first rugby World Cup.
He was just 22 and a veteran of only seven games for an England side which at the time belonged firmly in the second division of international rugby.

In some respects Carling was fortunate. He was surrounded by a group of like-minded players and had in manager Geoff Cooke a man who was also heartily sick of being patronised by the rest of the rugby world.
Carling began the first of his world record 59 tests as captain with a famous 28-19 victory over Australia.
"Everyone involved that day sensed something special, that a great corner had been turned," fly-half Rob Andrew recalled.
Under Carling, England quickly became an international force, playing some breathtaking rugby in 1990 before coming to grief in the grand slam finale at Murrayfield.

England that day appeared to believe in their own publicity, scorning goal-kicking options in favour of ultimately unsuccessful tap penalties and for the only time in his captaincy Carling did not appear to be in full control of his team.
No such hubris attended the 1991 World Cup year as England ground their way to a grand slam and qualified for the World Cup final where they lost to Australia.
There were to be three grand slams in all before Carling stood down in 1996, going on to play a final season under Phil de Glanville.

Just as significantly, Carling oversaw the transition to the professional era, taking full advantage of the commercial opportunities now available to top rugby players, and also played a leading role in the rise of player power.
He was sacked in 1995 just before the third World Cup for offensive remarks about the English Rugby Union but then reinstated after a player revolt.
Off the field a relationship with the Princess of Wales hit the front pages of the tabloids and contributed to the break-up of his marriage.
On the field, Carling never faltered.
By the highest standards he was not one of the world's great centres, losing his test place in the 1993 British Lions' side in New Zealand.
But he was consistently one of the best, a master of the half-break with the strength to stay upright in the tackle.
Defence, though, was always his strongest suit, notably on a memorable Twickenham day in 1993 when he stood firm in the face of wave after wave of attacks as England upset the New Zealand All Blacks.
"What always stood out for me was Will's sheer mental toughness, his determination to be the best" said Cooke. "He was a winner."
